item.title: The DC-Silicon Valley anti-China coalition is falling apart
item.description:
Arriving in the White House in 2021, President Joe Biden set about dismantling much of his predecessor’s foreign-policy agenda. But there was one clear area of continuity: China.

Here, Biden retained the first Trump administration’s confrontational approach, expanding the use of export controls on advanced technology and keeping China as the U.S. military’s pacing threat. In a time of deep political division, the newly formed China consensus appeared all-powerful. When the House voted in January 2023 to establish a select committee on “Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party,” the tally was 365 to 65.

Once President Donald Trump returned to power, observers expected more of the same. But Trump has instead moved U.S. China policy in the opposite direction, seeking to de-escalate bilateral tension in favor of “constructive strategic stability” and revealing that the bipartisan consensus on the “China threat” may be more ephemeral than many assumed.

Indeed, there is good reason to believe the peak of anti-China sentiment in U.S. politics has passed.

China’s place as the primary U.S. strategic competitor has its roots back in the early 2000s, but the narrative really took hold during Trump’s first term, when it won support from five different groups.

The first group was Trump’s Rust Belt base, to whom he and others supplied a narrative that scapegoated China for the economic and social dislocation they had suffered. China was also blamed for deaths of despair, including overdoses caused by fentanyl, whose precursor chemicals often came from China.

This groundswell against globalization was seized upon by a second group, made up of critics of the conventional economic case for global free trade: Trump himself, Peter Navarro, and Robert Lighthizer. Beginning in 2018, they imposed tariffs on some $360 billion of Chinese imports. The Biden administration maintained and entrenched this departure from free-trade globalism, announcing a “worker-centered” trade policy and reviving a U.S. industrial policy. Between them, the two administrations made bipartisan a shift away from the previous economic orthodoxy toward one focused on competitive trade with China.

The third group consisted of the foreign-policy establishment of liberal internationalists and conservative hawks. For this group, China filled a gap in U.S. foreign policy that had been empty since the end of the Cold War: the foreign adversary against which the U.S. could organize a global security bloc. In Trump’s first term, the role fell to the administration’s primacists and their allies – John Bolton, Matt Pottinger, and Mike Pompeo, who went to the Nixon Library in July 2020 to call for “a new alliance of democracies.” Two years later, Biden’s National Security Strategy called China “the only competitor with both the intent to reshape the international order and, increasingly, the economic, diplomatic, military, and technological power to advance that objective.” Accordingly, Biden and his national security team set about trying to contain Chinese power.

The fourth group contributing to the anti-China consensus were the offensive realists, such as John Mearsheimer and Elbridge Colby. Although they explicitly positioned themselves against the China hawks on both sides of the aisle who viewed the adversary through more ideological framings, they converged on a preference for slowing China’s rise. This cohort came to fear that China’s growing military capabilities and ambitions posed a direct threat to U.S. interests in East Asia. In response, they urged the United States to double down on its military investments in Asia to preserve U.S. advantages where they still existed.

Silicon Valley was the fifth and final group. Though initially skeptical of national allegiances and defense contracts, America’s technologists came around in the late 2010s, when new business interests and renewed geopolitical competition changed their calculus. In November 2017, Eric Schmidt, the former Google chief executive and a prominent Democratic donor, told an audience in Washington that China would catch up with the United States by 2020 and “dominate the industries of AI” by 2030.

Silicon Valley’s few Republicans fully embraced the geopolitical turn. Palmer Luckey founded Anduril in 2017 to build defense technology for the Pentagon. Peter Thiel and Alex Karp took Palantir public in 2020 with a filing that declared working with the Chinese Communist Party “inconsistent with our culture and mission.” Before long, this position transformed from taboo to commonplace. By the 2024 presidential election, Silicon Valley had bet on a combination of Trumpian nationalism and anti-China alarmism. There were holdouts, Nvidia and Apple among them, but they were now fighting the discourse rather than shaping it.

For much of the last decade, alignment among these groups created a seemingly unshakeable anti-China consensus. Yet the common thread was always made up of separate strands, whose unwinding should come as no surprise. Each group had its own reason for diagnosing China as a menace and has now found its own reasons to move in the other direction.

For starters, although China still receives much of the blame for the economic dislocation of American workers, it was always only one villain in the story – and the most distant. Other competitors for the same slot have come to dominate domestic discussion: migrants, “woke” elites, and other assorted culture-war enemies have all been held responsible for the plight of America’s dispossessed, displacing China as a sole focus of concern.

The trade hawks have also had to temper their zeal. The second Trump administration came in boasting about tariffs, with real trade warriors in key positions: Navarro at the White House, Jamieson Greer at USTR, Howard Lutnick at Commerce. “Liberation Day,” on April 2, 2025, was the big move. Within a week, the tariff on Chinese goods stood at 145%; but this effort hit a wall when China restricted its exports of rare earth metals. Since then, both sides have sought to de-escalate in the economic domain. The Trump administration still professes a desire for some rebalancing but has settled on a renewable trade truce as acceptable for now.

The liberal internationalists and neoconservatives continue to advocate a global containment strategy, but their influence is waning. While they still represent the largest cohort in Congress and occupy many think tank sinecures, they no longer dictate the terms of discussion. Their arguments have also started to fall flat abroad. “Allies and partners” who see relative U.S. decline are in no rush to back Washington and alienate Beijing, preferring instead to hedge.

The China threat remains central to the realist prioritizers, but they, too, have been forced to moderate their position. China’s military rise and the failed U.S. war with Iran have hastened the shift in the bilateral military balance while forcing a reevaluation of what the United States military can realistically achieve in Asia. Since the U.S. cannot afford a war with China in the medium term, realist prioritizers have started to shift the goal, from the pursuit of dominance to a “decent peace.”

Finally, the tech elite has softened somewhat on China. Jensen Huang and Nvidia were attacked in Congress, by both parties, for wanting to sell chips to China, but won the argument in the White House. The administration reversed its ban on the H20 chip in July 2025 and approved sales of the more powerful H200 in December, in exchange for a share of the revenue.

Meanwhile, the general public has decisively rejected the argument that an AI race with China requires all-out support for Silicon Valley. Polls show widespread support for AI regulation and broad opposition to the construction of data centers. American skepticism of Silicon Valley has so far eclipsed any anxiety over Chinese technological advancement.

Beyond the shifting perspectives of these five groups, the American public’s fatigue with confrontational foreign policy is also a factor. The public reaction to the war with Iran underscores the limited tolerance voters have for the disruption caused by unnecessary conflict.

None of these changes guarantees peaceful U.S.-China relations going forward. Despite recent leader-level summits filled with ceremony, the two sides continue to compete intensely in the security and economic domains. U.S.-China interactions will continue to be contentious for some time.

Still, the unraveling of the ad hoc coalition that created the apparent anti-China consensus makes any form of “new cold war” unlikely — and creates the potential for a real change in how the United States approaches China over the next decade.

item.title: Brett McGurk's account of Biden Gaza policy has a huge blind spot
item.description:
In April 2024, an Israeli drone struck a humanitarian convoy in Gaza, killing seven aid workers with World Central Kitchen, the food relief organization founded by celebrity chef Jose Andres.

A phone call between Biden and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyau days later was perhaps the closest Washington and Israel came to a rupture during the president’s term, according to Brett McGurk, the coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa in the Biden National Security Council.

At the time, intelligence indicated that Iran was preparing to launch drones and missiles at Israel in retaliation for the bombing of an Iranian consulate in Damascus on the same day as the WCK strike. “If not for the pending attack from Iran, we may have taken irreversible measures against Israel at this juncture,” McGurk writes in his recent book “Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages,” calling Biden as frustrated and angry as he’d ever seen him. But the president did not go further.

Though McGurk — one of a small group of key foreign-policy decision makers in the Biden White House — says he “wrestled” with whether cracking down on Israel was the right course of action at that time, his conclusion not to was firm.

Biden ultimately said that U.S. policy will be “determined by our assessment of Israel’s immediate action on … specific, concrete measurable steps to address civilian harm,” and days later he deployed the U.S. military to help defend Israel against the Iranian attack. “If there was a better way to end the crisis, whether at this moment or another, Biden would have taken it,” McGurk writes.

Threatening to cut off assistance and even “increasing public pressure” would have been detrimental, he insists. “It seemed to encourage those fighting against it,” He added that Tehran attacked Israel in part because it saw Washington under pressure to break with Tel Aviv.

Nearly two years after Biden shuffled out of office, McGurk is hard at work trying to paint the administration’s Gaza policy as the best response to a hopelessly complex crisis. The World Central Kitchen episode is one of many instances in which McGurk argues that public disagreements between Washington and Israel only served to strengthen their adversaries, undermining efforts to secure a ceasefire and the release of hostages held by Hamas. As a result, McGurk suggests Washington had few, if any, viable alternatives to the approach Biden and his team pursued.

While “Brink” also chronicles the regional conflicts that arose following Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, including in Iran and on the Red Sea, its central focus is McGurk’s painstaking efforts to negotiate the release of the hostages taken by Hamas on October 7. Throughout the book, he portrays any perceived daylight between the U.S. and Israel as counterproductive to his diplomatic endeavors, and places the responsibility for the prolonged conflict overwhelmingly on Hamas. But former Biden administration officials who served alongside McGurk challenge that framing, arguing that his account disregards both the potential benefits of pressuring Israel and the costs of Washington's reluctance to do so.

As one former Biden administration official said, pressure on Israel actually helped secure concessions from Hamas by giving Arab governments greater political latitude to press the militant group themselves.

"When the United States demonstrated that it was also willing to exert pressure on the party over which it had the most influence, Israel, then the Arab countries were actually able to really turn the screws," the official told RS, pointing to Egypt and Turkey's key roles in the negotiations during the Biden-Trump transition, and later in the implementation of the framework signed in October 2025.

And even when American pressure failed to advance the hostage negotiations, it could achieve other objectives. Speaking about that tense April 2024 phone call in which, according to McGurk, Biden threatened to cut off military aid, Ilan Goldenberg offered a different assessment of its consequences. Where McGurk laments the potential dangers of confronting Israel, Goldenberg, who served as a Middle East adviser to Vice President Kamala Harris, says “that is only if you view this purely as a hostage negotiation and you forget all about the Palestinian humans.”

Following this intervention, Israel agreed to the temporary reopening of the Erez Crossing, and April 2024 saw the most truckloads of humanitarian supplies enter the strip of any month between October 2023 and January 2025, according to United Nations data. This represented a “fundamental change,” according to Goldenberg, one that did not last long because Washington failed to keep up the pressure.

The narrow focus on the hostage negotiations runs throughout “Brink.” McGurk devotes considerable attention to the hostages and their families, whereas the suffering of Palestinians, while acknowledged, receives far less attention, with the devastation in Gaza —where roughly 46,000 people were killed by the time Biden left office in 2025, according to health officials in the strip — largely treated as a backdrop to his diplomatic efforts.

Whether greater American pressure could have helped bring about an earlier ceasefire — one that would have freed the hostages — remains a contentious question.

Examining Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar's conduct throughout the war, there was little evidence his willingness to reach a deal was meaningfully influenced by disagreements between Washington and Israel, said the former official who spoke with RS.

“He was singularly focused on maximizing the pain on Israel,” the official said, so it simply “doesn’t add up” that he would be responsive to outside events.

Another member of the Biden administration, speaking on condition of anonymity, argued that even if public pressure risked emboldening Hamas, Washington's reluctance to confront Netanyahu carried risks of its own, giving the Israeli prime minister latitude on how to conduct negotiations even as he seemed to want the war to continue. McGurk’s perspective instead emphasizes the times when Hamas is an intransigent negotiating partner while glossing over times when Netanyahu impedes talks.

That issue becomes particularly relevant in the author’s treatment of the failed efforts to secure a ceasefire in the summer of 2024.

In late May 2024, McGurk says, Netanyahu accepted a phased ceasefire and hostage release framework that Biden had endorsed. Hamas took more than a month to respond, a delay McGurk highlights as evidence of the group's unwillingness to compromise. “Hamas did not care at all about the plight of Gazans; it only cared about its own survival,” he wrote.

Phil Gordon, who served as Harris's national security adviser, challenged McGurk's account earlier this month, arguing Hamas's eventual response in early July represented a significant concession: the group had dropped its demand that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released.

“That felt to us like a significant step forward. Nobody was naive in thinking that this wouldn't be difficult,” Gordon recently told the Jerusalem Post.

In “Brink,” McGurk describes Hamas’s response as containing “about two dozen substantive amendments to a carefully negotiated text,” many of which were “unworkable.” The ceasefire plan was further derailed, he adds, because “new issues had also arisen.”

These “new issues” refer to Netanyahu's sudden insistence on maintaining an Israeli military presence along the recently-seized Philadelphi Corridor, on Gaza’s border with Egypt, and introducing a screening mechanism for Palestinians returning to northern Gaza. Other administration officials say these demands came during a July 4 phone call with Biden, and despite the U.S. president’s push to persuade Netanyahu to move forward with the agreement. That phone call is not specifically mentioned in “Brink.”

“In the book, Brett says the situation on the ground changed and therefore the Israelis had new requirements,” Goldenberg told RS. “That's a very coded way of saying when Biden got on the phone and said to take the deal, Bibi said no.” One Israeli former hostage negotiator has said that July 2024 represented a missed chance to secure the hostages’ release, because he “didn’t think the Philadelphi Corridor was so important that it was right to miss the window of opportunity because of it.”

The new Israeli conditions proved to not be immovable. In the eventual agreement, struck in January 2025, the IDF agreed to withdraw from the corridor, though Israel has refused to follow through on that part of the agreement.

McGurk disputes the analysis that Israeli concessions were ultimately what made the agreement possible. In a book talk at the Atlantic Council this month, he called that suggestion “totally not true” and maintained that Hamas had finally accepted terms it had rejected the previous summer, driven in part by Israel’s military victories and the death of Sinwar.

McGurk occasionally acknowledges Netanyahu was an obstacle to peace, describing the prime minister during closing stages of hostage negotiations as “the flip side of Hamas,” because he would delay potential agreements, believing that prolonging the war would strengthen his negotiating position. But this doesn’t seem to affect his thinking on whether it made sense to pressure the Israeli prime minister.

The final chapters of “Brink,” however, suggest that a change in the U.S. approach also played a decisive role in the January 2025 hostage deal. Steve Witkoff, the incoming Trump administration's Middle East envoy, joins McGurk in the final negotiations. With a deal nearly complete, Witkoff aggressively presses Netanyahu to increase the number of Palestinian prisoners who would be released in exchange for nine sick or injured civilian hostages, in the first part of a larger deal.

At one point, McGurk recounts his replacement as telling the head of Mossad “tell your prime minister this is over (...) or I’ll go out right now and say the Israelis don’t give two shits about their hostages.” Ultimately, the Israeli prime minister relented.

Is Europe starting to come to its senses on Ukraine?
item.description:
The Trump administration’s latest initiative to end the war is creating heartburn in Europe.

“We have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender,” said European Union High Representative Kaja Kallas. “Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that's why Europe is standing by Ukraine.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, insists Russia has no genuine desire for peace, pointing in particular to Russian strikes on Ukrainian civilians.

This moral language frames the conflict as a zero-sum, good-versus-evil struggle. In this light, Europeans have no choice but to unite behind Ukraine to stop Russian President Vladimir Putin.

But not all European leaders are talking this way. Last Tuesday’s press conference in Oslo featuring Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb was full of constructive language about ending the conflict. Stubb said the Oslo summit was the result of "substantive progress" made "under the radar." Støre emphasised that "Europe has to be at the table" to secure a "lasting peace." Europe, it seems, is not united on a negotiated end to the conflict.

The Oslo summit is no bolt from the blue; Finnish and Norwegian representatives have been preparing the ground for several months. At last week’s Warsaw Security Forum, Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide avoided the usual binary of Ukraine’s victory or capitulation. He stressed that since the Europeans are now paying for the war, they should also lead the diplomacy to end it. Eide noted that a peace agreement could secure a democratic, independent Ukraine integrated into the EU with 80% of its original territory. Advancing this point among more hawkish European colleagues, Eide struck a tone of hope rather than fear. In an interview last Saturday, Eide noted that Europe must contribute concrete proposals for a post-war security architecture: "in the long run, we need to return to a normal relationship with Russia after the war (....) some kind of order must be restored.”

During his recent visit to the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs, Stubb presented a complementary argument. Restating his case for a “value-based realism,” he argued that European states should be faithful to their values but would not resolve the conflict by rigidly clinging to the moral high ground. Stubb urged the audience to keep “cooler heads”; fostering a “war mentality” would make it near impossible to conceive of peace.

Eide and Stubb are moving in a different direction from those who claim “victory” over Russia – however defined – is a prerequisite for future European security. They reject the mantra of ex-NATO Secretary General Stoltenberg that “weapons are the way to peace” and emphasize the military reality that neither side has the resources to win decisively.

This is a noble recognition of reality. Offensive actions from both sides have repeatedly failed to produce a breakthrough. Costs keep rising for both warring parties, while gains have become increasingly meagre. Europe, Ukraine, and Russia are stuck in a war that cannot be won on the terms set by either side.

Continuing the current course brings problems for all sides. Putin faces an overheating economy and increasing social fatigue and anxiety. Even if Russia destroys more and more Ukrainian infrastructure from the air, land offensives are likely to incur heavy losses. Ukraine's situation is even tougher. Its chronic manpower shortages have led to intensified forced mobilization and increased social strains. Blockaded at sea and bombarded from the air, Ukraine is also short of money and weapons, constantly appealing to Western allies to plug the gaps.

The European coalition behind Ukraine faces serious problems of its own. Many European states are facing a sovereign debt crisis as war costs mount. The EU has been unable to persuade Belgium to make use of Russia’s frozen assets to fund the war. All the while, the dirty reality is that, since the war began, Europe has spent more on Russian energy imports than on weapons for Ukraine.

At the same time, Ukraine’s campaign of intensified deep strikes on Russia – supported by the Europeans and greenlit by the Trump Administration in spring 2026 – has failed to pressure Putin into a ceasefire. Without U.S. intelligence and weapons supplies, Europe lacks the military leverage to continue this effort on its own. There is no viable European war plan, only reactive crisis management and ad hoc solutions about Ukraine, coupled with repeated hyping of Russia’s “hybrid war” threat.

Tuesday’s meeting in Oslo provides a way out of this mess. As Stubb said at Tuesday’s press conference: “Peace requires patience. But unfortunately, war does not wait. People are dying each and every day. Our job is to do what we can to end it.” Norway and Finland are communicating the urgency of ending a senseless war. Referring to the recent spat between Trump and Zelensky, Støre advised against dwelling on past disagreements: “What matters now is what lies ahead of us.”

On the same day, Kaja Kallas looked back in anger. She accused the Trump administration of trying to “push Ukraine into surrender” on “Putin’s terms.” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, for her part, presented Ukraine as Europe’s only protection: “If we allow Ukraine to fall, we will open the way for Russia to advance into other parts of Europe.”

One can understand fears that, if Ukraine is rendered neutral with limits on its armed forces, Russia would hold the whip hand over Europe. Nobody wants to let Moscow dictate the terms of the European security architecture through violence. But at this point, Europe’s rejection of a “dirty deal” could mean impotently watching Ukraine’s destruction over the next six months. How would this outcome improve European security or prestige?

Norway and Finland have offered the most constructive European response to U.S. diplomacy since Trump returned to the White House. They offer Europe a new language of patient diplomacy to replace maximalist rhetoric. This is in line with both countries’ previous experience mediating and building bridges with Russia. It also recognizes a basic fact: all protracted wars not settled decisively on the battlefield — which is to say, the vast majority of wars — end in negotiated settlements between the aggressor and the defender. America’s signature is absolutely necessary to secure such an outcome.

Mainstream analysis seems unable to accept these realities. It is stuck in moral posturing or fearmongering. There is still little serious discussion of what compromises might be struck. The 28-point plan that U.S.-Russian diplomacy developed in 2025 should not be equated with Ukraine’s capitulation, nor is it a recipe for turning Ukraine into Belarus. Ukraine would enter the EU, receive reconstruction assistance, and retain armed forces on a level comparable to Finland's. It is time to return to the core points on which a deal must be struck.

Russia has responded positively to the proposals sent from Oslo. Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. have agreed to a three-way summit in November, according to Zelensky. The key question now is whether other European governments will take the Oslo initiative seriously and agree on who can represent Europe in these talks. Dmitri Peskov, Putin’s press secretary, has cautiously welcomed the idea that Alexander Stubb could represent Europe in the negotiations.

Finland and Norway’s more moderate language is a crucial first step toward a shared European understanding that continuing the war in its current form is self-defeating. As the Eide observed at the U.N. last month, “diplomacy can work – if we allow it to.”

But first, Europe must decide: will it support or sabotage the U.S. effort to build a diplomatic off-ramp?

Why America’s Military Still Needs Its Allies
item.description:
“We never fight alone. We've never done that. You can go all the way back to the days of Revolutionary War. The United States has never gone into conflict on its own. We've always built coalitions. We've always involved partners and allies. And we'll continue to do so going forward.”

That was Gen. Ronald P. Clark, Commanding General, U.S. Army Pacific Command, speaking last Tuesday at a contemporary military forum, Decisive Landpower -- Deterrence and Partner Integration Against the Pacing Threat, as part of the 2026 Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Conference in Washington, D.C.

On the panel with Clark was Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, Commander, United Nations Command, U.S. Forces Korea, and Tara Murphy Dougherty, Chief Executive Officer of Air, a leading AI software firm that specializes in national security readiness.

The two Army generals spent a good deal of their time talking about lessons learned from Ukraine and the benefits to the U.S. of allies – specifically in the Pacific. That struck me as something to further explore, since one day later, on Wednesday, President Trump continued his running criticism of allies with an October 14, Truth Social screed.

Trump said in part: “Because of the fact that we have had such Military Success, we no longer ‘need,’ or desire, the NATO Countries’ assistance — WE NEVER DID! Likewise, Japan, Australia, or South Korea. In fact, speaking as President of the United States of America, by far the Most Powerful Country Anywhere in the World, WE DO NOT NEED THE HELP OF ANYONE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

On the other hand, Gen. Brunson had told the AUSA audience one day earlier, “Everything that we do is intricately woven around the ROK (Republic of Korea)-U.S. alliance. That alliance has stood for some 75 years and it is an example or a paragon, if you will, of all that's right when folk work in alliance together. The problems that we solve are joint problems. They're not just U.S. problems. They're not just Republic of Korea problems. What they are is great opportunities for two nations to work in concert with one another in order to arrive at solutions that are beneficial for both countries.”

Gen. Clark explained further, “So our ability to be able to work with partners and allies on their sovereign soil, to be able to share procedures that we build through [military] exercises over the course of a year, some joint, some army-to-army, but always integrated with our partners. It gives us the opportunity to have our systems work technically, to have our procedures nested, and to get to know one another in a way that allows us to build the trust that's necessary in training. Because if we wait until crisis or conflict, it's too late to ask the question, can I trust

you? But because we've been working together, because we've exercised at scale, because we're modernizing our forces alongside one another, it works.”

Clark added, “We've really worked hard at building those relationships at scale inside of the land forces. We have a land forces dialogue that meets multiple times a year -- chiefs of army of Australia, Japan, the Philippines, and the U.S. We've invited the ROKs in, we've invited India in, and it continues to grow. So those relationships built army-to-army are what allows us to really integrate across interoperability, and integrate it really across our formations and with our partners in all.”

Brunson described how he and Korean Gen. Kim Sung-min, Deputy Commander of the U.S.-ROK Combined Forces Command, discussed training differently “taking advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight.”

Brunson said, “We talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion…Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the [Korean] Peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say you can't utilize the things that you've learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learned the same lessons and we've distributed ourselves in such a way that we don't make ourselves the target. We won't be moored in place.”

Clark talked about Russia, North Korea and China “learning from watching us partner, but the partnerships that our adversaries have built are transactional versus the transformational relationships that we build as a security partner of choice globally…for us it's really transformational relationships that we look to cultivate with partners and allies over time.”

Brunson described how the North Koreans, fighting for the Russians in Ukraine were “able to test systems there…and then bring that back home. So, in one aspect, they've shortened their RDT&E cycle.” He also pointed out, “The fact that you have a combat trained force with recent

combat on the [Korean] Peninsula for the first time since 1953..[and] are now bringing those lessons learned back into their own training cycle, it's shortened their time to develop them.”

Clark said that U.S. forces had also learned from Ukraine about the need for mobility and camouflage, which he described as “age-old army forgotten sciences of how to hide in plain sight and how to camouflage ourselves from observation...Our ability to be able to use electronic warfare, to be able to use just good, old-fashioned camouflage and the ability to deceive our adversary is a must. In those two theaters [Ukraine and Iran] it's not a near-peer adversary that we would be working against -- whereas, in our theater [the Pacific] it absolutely is.”

For Clark, the questions were: “How do we fight, you know, Type One, Type Two UAS [unmanned aerial system, drones]; how do we think through ballistic missile defense holistically in the region. We spend a lot of time working again with the joint force for solutions associated with that. How do we maneuver?”

Brunson raised a new issue by pointing out that, “Our old system was something [a weapons system] breaks, we send it all the way back CONUS [Continental U.S.] in order to fix it so we can then bring it all the way back out again.” That used to take 29 days by ship.

However, he added, “In the ally that we have in Korea we have a an absolutely premier industrial base, if you look at the Korea defense industry, some of the kit that we're producing right now sits along our friends, allies and partners.” Brunson said, “The Army’s new infantry squad vehicle (ISV), for example, is produced by GM Defense and GM Defense is also in the Republic of Korea.”

“So the idea of a regional sustainment hub would simply be…to bring those means of production to the theater,” Brunson suggested, noting, “In the maritime domain, when we look at maintenance, repair, and overhaul, which is being done forward alongside the Koreans, you know that 15 percent of global ship building is done in Korea. And, oh by the way, we've got an ally with a mutual defense treaty in Japan that has 10% of global ship building. And if we take these cases forward, we're able to stay in theater longer.”

The answer, Brunson said, “We've got to try to achieve admirable endurance in theater by partnering alongside our allies, seeing the things that they can do better than we can right now at distance and then keeping them right where they belong. That keeps our [military] forces forward.”

Dougherty chipped in saying: “Tens of millions of dollars saved by simply identifying things like unfilled requisitions or parts that are obsolete that can be replaced with something not obsolete and also less expensive. I think that this is it. This is part of how you generate lethality. You get readiness to pay for itself, because otherwise sustainment is too expensive when it has to be done for the entirety of the joint force all the way on the other side of the world.”

At one point, Clark said, “The secret sauce for us as an Army is our Non-Commissioned Officer (NCO) corps, reflecting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s September 30 speech praising the same group.

Clark noted that both he and Brunson were sons of NCOs, and that “with the assistance of our senior non-commissioned officers, senior enlisted leaders across the [PACOM] region have embarked upon conducting assessments with our partners and developing strategies to help them build their NCO development programs inside of their formations.”

To illustrate his point, Clark said his units had just finished an assessment in Cambodia of its army and the Commander, Gen. Mao Sophan, “basically said, ‘Hey, whatever you're asking us to do, we're going to do it because we want to get to a level of proficiency with our Non-Commissioned Officer core that we see in yours.’"

I must point out that during the one-hour-and-thirty-minute session neither General -- Clark nor Brunson -- came near to mentioning President Trump’s repeated critical views about U.S. allies.

The closest anyone came was Dougherty, who at one point said diplomatically, “We'll head into midterm elections here [in the U.S.] in November, obviously as you know, and I think we expect some variation in the political dynamic in the United States, and our allies and partners all navigate their own political changes as well.”

She then added, “If you look over the course of history, however, at least modern history, certainly the United States has invested in those partnerships. And today, we still are -- maybe with a different flavor or a different attitude. And that's not really for me to say. I'm simply observing. But we haven't lost sight of the importance of allies and partners to securing U.S. national interests.”

I would bet Clark and Brunson – along with most U.S. military professionals – would silently agree with her statement.

item.title: Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited
item.description:
Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited Expert comment thilton.drupal 27 October 2026

Russia’s footprint in Africa has expanded in recent years, but engagement beyond security remains uneven. The summit alone is unlikely to change this.

The third Russia–Africa Summit, which was initially announced to take place in Libya, will now take place in Moscow on 28–29 October. The summit is being portrayed as a test of Russia’s growing influence across Africa. 

Once again, considerable emphasis is being placed on how many African leaders will be attending the gathering. The Kremlin says 22 African heads of state are attending, a slight increase on the 17 that attended the summit’s second edition in St Petersburg in 2023. That marked a significant decrease from the 43 leaders that were present at the inaugural summit in Sochi in 2019. Then, the Kremlin attributed the lower turnout to ‘outrageous’ Western pressure. 

Attendance at the summit, however, is a poor measure of durable partnerships. This is particularly the case as the constraints of Russia’s partnership have become harder for African governments to overlook. 

While Russian engagement with Africa has expanded in recent years, its economic delivery remains limited and the outcomes of its security role in the Sahel have been uneven. The summit may therefore lead to new agreements, but with the war in Ukraine still constraining Russia’s resources, it is unlikely to change these fundamental dynamics. 

Summit priorities

Russia’s interest in Africa reflects its own priorities. These include countering Western influence, building non-aligned partnerships and advancing multilateral reform. Expanding defence sales, securing minerals access and mitigating the impact of sanctions are also priorities. 

Moscow has pursued these objectives partly by using the BRICS grouping, which includes South Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia. It has also maintained its own bilateral political, security and economic relationships.

The summit, which will be accompanied by an economic and humanitarian forum, speaks directly to Moscow’s interests while also responding to African priorities. It is expected to promote new payment systems, reform of global financial institutions, stronger African representation at international organizations and opposition to unilateral sanctions. It will also discuss trade and investment, food and energy security, nuclear energy, technology and security cooperation. 

The summit is expected to produce a joint declaration, a separate declaration on AI cooperation, and an action plan for 2027–2029.

Russia’s deepening footprint

Security has been one of Russia’s main focuses in Africa. Since 2023, Africa Corps – the Russian state-controlled paramilitary force that replaced the Wagner Group – has expanded its presence. It has deployed beyond Mali, the Central African Republic and Libya to Burkina Faso and Niger. There are also reports pointing at possible deployments in Togo, which signed a military cooperation agreement with Moscow in 2025.

As insurgent attacks persist in the Sahel, Russia has deepened its ties with the Alliance of Sahel States (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger), pledging military and technical support. The three states have increasingly turned to Russia for security and diplomatic support following their break from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), and amid deteriorating relations with Western partners. Russia is also pursuing a parallel security cooperation agreement with ECOWAS, which will cover the broader region. 

Related work

Mali attacks show security cannot be delivered by military means alone

Diplomatically, Moscow has expanded its network of embassies on the continent, with planned missions bringing the total to 49. Russia has also sought to extend its diplomatic reach to the Horn of Africa amid rising tensions there, offering to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea on the margins of the summit in Moscow. The proposal signals Moscow’s ambition to position itself as a security interlocutor beyond the Sahel, although it remains an offer rather than a confirmed mediation effort.

Russia has also sought to deepen its economic footprint in Africa. Russian agricultural exports to Africa grew 35 percent in value in the first half of 2026, to $2.9 billion, with wheat shipments reaching record volumes. 

It has signed intergovernmental nuclear cooperation agreements with at least 15 African states.  For example, Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear corporation, signed an agreement to build a nuclear power plant in Ethiopia.   

Russia is also working with the African Union. At a July 2026 consultation in Addis Ababa, both sides committed to annual high-level political consultations and to launch sectoral dialogues. 

Limited returns

However, despite Russia’s deepening involvement in sectors such as energy and agricultural exports, trade between Africa and Russia is estimated at $27 billion in 2025, well below the $40 billion target announced by Putin in 2019.  It also pales in comparison to the EU’s €355 billion ($395 billon) and China’s $348 billion of recorded trade with Africa in 2025. 

In June, Russia’s foreign ministry acknowledged at a forum in St Petersburg that previous summits had produced more declaration than deals. It promised this third summit will be different.  

Related work

Can Africa maximize its global influence?

Agreements on nuclear power are yet to translate into completed projects. Egypt’s El Dabaa plant is still under construction. Ethiopia’s nuclear power plant is still at a prospective stage. 

Even in defence, the picture is not favourable. Russian global arms exports declined by 64 percent in 2021-2025. Russia ranked third, behind the US and China, in major arms supply to Africa during the same period. 

Russia’s increased security role in the Sahel has also failed to deliver reliable security guarantees. Annual deaths linked to violent extremism in the Sahel have increased from an average of 927 in 2016–2019 to an average of 10,470 in 2022–2025. 

In April 2026, a coalition of Tuareg separatists and al-Qaeda-linked jihadists killed Mali’s defence Minister and forced Africa Corps personnel to withdraw from the northern city of Kidal. Russian-backed forces subsequently regained control of Kidal in October, but the episode has exposed the limits of their security model. 

Russian-linked actors have sought to offset the costs of the war through security-for-resources arrangements, including control of and revenue from African gold mines; the US Treasury reports that gold and other African resources have helped Russia evade sanctions and fund its military efforts in Ukraine. 

There is also the question of the extent to which Russia can sustain its security commitments in Africa while its resources and attention remain stretched by the war in Ukraine.

Recruiting for the Ukraine war

Russia’s recruitment of African citizens to fight in Ukraine has become a reputational liability. A recent investigation cited by African media outlets estimated that more than 3,000 African citizens from 40 countries were recruited into Russia’s armed forces between October 2022 and June 2026, often through deception and promises of civilian jobs. Bloomberg reported this week that Moscow has been widening its recruitment drive in countries including Zimbabwe, Burundi and Sierra Leone. 

Related work

After Trump’s Russian diesel deal, will Europe give Ukraine the support it needs? 

African countries including Kenya and South Africa have sought to stop the recruitment of their citizens. During a visit to Moscow in April, Kenya’s foreign minister Musalia Mudavadi said that Moscow and Nairobi had agreed that Kenyan nationals would no longer be enlisted by Russia’s ministry of defence. Russia’s embassy in Nairobi had denied any involvement in recruitment.

An Afrobarometer survey of citizens across 38 African countries in 2024–2025 found that the perception of Russian influence was far less positive than that of China, the US, the EU and others, and 72 per cent of those who had heard of the Ukraine war wanted their country to remain neutral in it.

From rhetoric to delivery

The pattern of African engagement with Russia is best understood as diversified non-alignment. African governments see Moscow as one of several partners with whom they can pursue their interests in trade, security and greater representation in international forums. 

With Russia’s capacity constrained by the war in Ukraine, which continues to drain resources and diplomatic bandwidth, the real test is whether Moscow can convert political declarations and security interests into concrete, deliverable commitments in other fields.

Ultimately, Russia’s standing as a partner will depend on its ability to provide sustained economic benefits, reliable security partnerships and tangible outcomes for African countries. The summit will indicate the scale of Moscow’s ambitions; the years that follow will reveal how far it can realistically meet them.

If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm

Following the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, she told one interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.

Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined their visions of a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally, proposes slashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.

F-35 Fallacy: Jets Alone Will Not Save Us
item.description:
NATO Allies have bet the future of European skies on the world’s most sophisticated combat aircraft. NATO Allies are buying the world's most advanced fighter but many are neglecting vital investments in hard security, ground crews, and support systems that will keep it flying.

By 2028, European flight lines will host upwards of 700 F-35 Lightning jets. On paper, this inventory represents an insurmountable technological edge: a sensor-fused, fifth-generation fleet that outmatches any potential adversary in radar-cross-section, situational awareness, and electronic attack.

Yet this procurement spree masks a dangerous complacency. The Alliance has poured vast capital into acquiring fifth-generation airframes while systematically underinvesting in the unglamorous terrestrial infrastructure that keeps them flying: base hardening, counter-drone defenses, resilient networks, and ground crews. An F-35 sitting on an unhardened runway without fuel, parts, or secure command links is not a deterrent, it is an expensive target.

The cockpit may deliver tactical lethality, but operational endurance is generated entirely on the tarmac. If conflict erupts with Russia, the fight for European airspace will look less like a sterile, high-tech turkey shoot and more like the grueling attrition of the Battle of Britain.

Surviving Day Zero

Historically, the most efficient method of destroying an air force has rarely been in air-to-air combat; it has been catching it on the ramp. Operation Focus in 1967 wiped out Egypt’s air force before breakfast. Conversely, Ukraine averted immediate disaster in February 2022 because it aggressively dispersed its scarce aircraft and mobile air-defense batteries hours before Russian cruise missiles slammed into permanent garrisons.

Recent innovations have further collapsed the boundary between frontline and rear sanctuary. In June 2025, Ukraine demonstrated the democratization of deep strike with Operation Spiderweb, deploying commercial-style drones smuggled deep into the Russian interior to strike strategic bombers parked in the open. The threat bypassed layered air defense belts entirely; it originated outside the airbase perimeter fence. Coupled with intelligence reports of sabotage devices targeting logistical hubs in Western Europe, such as the attempted strikes near Leipzig, the implication for NATO is clear: rear sanctuary no longer exists.

Russia has studied these dynamics carefully. A coordinated "Day Zero" assault will not rely solely on long-range Iskander or Kalibr barrages. It will combine standoff salvos with covert proxy drone launches, special reconnaissance sabotage, and electromagnetic disruption targeting key airbases before any formal declaration of Article 5. If NATO’s F-35 fleet remains concentrated at sprawling, unhardened hubs, the Alliance risks losing the air war before its pilots can take off.

Survival on Day Zero will not come from a single system. Ground-based air defense will kill aircraft, cruise missiles will crater runways, and drones will hunt anything left in the open. The answer is dispersal, concealment, and resilience, practiced and exercised daily long before the shooting starts.

A Battle of Britain, Not a High-Tech War in the Air

The operational template NATO must internalize is not Desert Storm, but southern England in the summer of 1940. When the Luftwaffe hammered RAF sector stations across Kent and Sussex - cratering Biggin Hill, Manston, and Kenley - the British survived because of an integrated, highly resilient system.

It was not the Spitfire alone that preserved Britain; it was the Dowding System. Radar stations, visual observers, filter rooms, and telephone lines fused intelligence into an actionable operational picture and directed scarce interceptors to precise intercept vectors. Crucially, the system was distributed and made redundant. When individual nodes went dark, the architecture adapted. Meanwhile, exhausted ground crews patched runways and re-armed aircraft under constant threat of bombardment.

NATO faces an analogous network challenge today. The F-35 is a formidable intelligence-collection platform, but its utility plummets if its Multifunction Advanced Data Link (MADL) cannot pass target tracks to legacy fourth-generation fighters, naval surface combatants, or ground-based air defenses under heavy electronic jamming. If a Combined Air Operations Center (CAOC) is knocked offline, who assumes control of the theater airspace? Without distributed, jam-resistant data architectures and mission command protocols for degraded environments, tactical technological dominance will dissolve into operational paralysis.

Operational Imperatives for NATO Airpower

If NATO intends to build genuine deterrence by denial, member states must balance platform acquisition with systemic survivability across five core areas:

  1. Institutionalize Dispersal and Agile Combat Employment (ACE): Finland and Sweden have long mastered highway-strip operations, rapid turnaround, and camouflage doctrine. These must cease to be High North novelties and become standard operating procedure across all Allied air forces. Peacetime operations must routinely exercise dispersed sortie generation from municipal airports and road networks.
  2. Harden the Perimeter and the Flight Line: Every euro invested in advanced airframes must be matched by funding for base survivability: point-defense against low-altitude UAS, hardened aircraft shelters, mobile arrestor gear, rapid airfield damage repair (RADR) kits, and deep magazines of precision munitions.
  3. Expand Logistics at Strategic Depth: Dispersed operating locations demand rapid logistics and robust aerial refueling capacity. Staging fighters farther from the contact line requires a dramatic expansion of NATO’s multinational tanker fleet and hardened pipeline distribution networks.
  4. Solve the Cross-Domain Data Mesh: Allies must field resilient, low-probability-of-intercept gateways that translate fifth-generation sensor data into common operational pictures accessible to non-stealth assets and ground-based integrated air and missile defense systems. They also need the ability to protect and secure their entire EW spectrum, given the F-35's massive reliance on it.
  5. Re-arm and Re-train the Ground Crew: The maintainer, armorer, and combat engineer are frontline combatants. NATO must equip ground personnel with specialized force-protection capabilities, chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear defense gear, and the cross-training required to generate combat sorties in austere, contested conditions.

The True Cost of Deterrence

Deterrence is not measured by the sophistication of one platform; it is measured by the credible ability to absorb a first strike and generate combat power under fire. Building that credibility requires realistic, high-tempo exercises in harsh weather, degraded communications environments, and austere road bases. It must be under conditions that carry legitimate operational risk and wear on equipment.

Before 1989, this operational friction was the routine cost of doing business in Allied Air Forces Central Europe. The pilots of 1940 earned their place in history, but unheralded mechanics, plotters, and engineers preserved their freedom to fight. As NATO retools for contested collective defense, it must remember that fifth-generation air power is only as resilient as the ground beneath its wheels.

item.title: Europe went from leading Iran diplomacy to slavishly following US
item.description:
There was a time when Europe was serious about diplomacy — diplomacy as the patient, often frustrating business of engaging adversaries, rather than merely issuing condemnations and imposing sanctions.

Ten years ago, on October 25, 2016, the European Parliament adopted a report on relations with Iran that embodied precisely this understanding of statecraft. Drafted under the leadership of British MEP Richard Howitt, it offered a forward-looking strategy for engaging Tehran following the conclusion of the 2015 nuclear agreement, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) – a diplomatic achievement in which the European Union and its member states the United Kingdom, France and Germany played a leading role.

As a foreign policy adviser in the European Parliament, I had the privilege of working closely with Howitt throughout the report’s preparation, negotiations, and eventual adoption, including a fact-finding mission to Tehran. The report was adopted by an overwhelming majority of 456 votes to 174, with 67 abstentions.

But its significance extended well beyond parliamentary numbers: it represented a moment when Europe appeared capable of acting with strategic foresight. The engagement with Iran was a pragmatic instrument for advancing European security and economic interests; fostering moderation in Iran; and stabilizing the Middle East.

Ten years later, EU-Iran relations are in tatters. Europe has lost much of its economic leverage, its diplomatic influence has diminished dramatically, and its role in addressing the region’s security crises has become marginal.

To understand the scale of this decline, one needs to look back at how pragmatic and ambitious Europe’s approach once was.

The Howitt report proposed developing relations in key areas, including political dialogue, trade,academic exchanges, human rights, and regional security. It offered European expertise to assist Iran in fulfilling the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) criteria – a key step toward economic reform.

The report departed from the mantra promoted for years by hawkish circles in the U.S., Israel and some Arab capitals, which had depicted Iran as the sole source of regional turmoil. Instead, it recognized Iran as an indispensable actor in addressing conflicts in Syria, Iraq, and Yemen. It called for European diplomacy to encourage rapprochement between Tehran and Riyadh – an appeal acted upon years later, by Beijing, not Brussels.

Crucially, the report did not remain a simple exercise in parliamentary rhetoric. Just a few weeks after its adoption, the EU Foreign Affairs Council endorsed the parliamentary approach for engagement with Tehran. It also supported the establishment of an EU delegation in Tehran. Here was a case where parliamentary diplomacy had contributed to shaping the broader political position of the EU.

Reactions to the report were revealing. The National Iranian American Council (NIAC), a Washington-based pro-diplomacy group, welcomed it enthusiastically. Its founder and then-president, Trita Parsi, now executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, praised the strategy of expanded relations while warning against renewed isolation and military threats.

Perhaps the best evidence of the report’s impact was its hostile reception by forces committed to confrontation. Pro-Israeli groups, such as the AJC Transatlantic Institute (TAI), the Brussels office of the American Jewish Committee, denounced the text for allegedly failing to confront Iran’s threats against Israel; its support for Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Assad regime in Syria; and its human rights abuses.

The false choice between defending human rights and engaging with Tehran was peddled relentlessly by the report’s critics. However, the report contained substantial criticism of Iran’s record in that area, including input from Human Rights Watch.

We proposed to anchor discussions on human rights in a broader framework of dialogue rather than simply issuing condemnations. As Howitt said during the parliamentary debate, addressing his critics, “they knowingly imperil the leverage that we do have with Iran and make the improvements in human rights less, not more, likely”.

Reactions from Tehran were equally instructive. The Foreign Ministry’s spokesman acknowledged that “a number of promising points exist in the document which can help open new horizons in and expand relations between the EU and Iran.”

Yet spoilers existed on the Iranian side, too. Mohammad Javad Larijani, then secretary-general of the Iranian judiciary’s High Council for Human Rights, objected to the establishment of an EU delegation in Tehran, suggesting it could interfere in Iran’s internal affairs.

The allegation was ludicrous: 22 of the EU’s then-28 member states, including the United Kingdom, already maintained embassies in Tehran, while the EU had delegations in numerous countries whose governments had profound disagreements with Brussels.

Larijani’s objection reflected a suspicion within parts of Iran’s political establishment that closer relations with the West would invite political subversion. This strengthened precisely those European voices that portrayed engagement with Tehran as futile or even dangerous.

In 2015 and 2016, however, the spoilers on both sides seemed unlikely to derail the positive trajectory. There was reason to believe that the JCPOA, in the view of the then-EU foreign policy chief, Federica Mogherini, was indeed only the floor, not the ceiling, for EU-Iran relations.

That optimism proved tragically short-lived.

When President Donald Trump unilaterally withdrew the U.S. from the JCPOA in 2018, despite international verification of Iran’s compliance at the time, the EU formally opposed Washington’s decision. But the gap between the EU’s declarations and its capacity to act to preserve the agreement soon became painfully obvious.

European companies withdrew from Iran under the threat of secondary U.S. sanctions. Banks refused transactions. The EU attempted to preserve trade through mechanisms such as INSTEX, but these proved woefully inadequate. The promised economic benefits for Iran of the agreement never materialized.

Meanwhile, in a misguided attempt to appease Trump, the E3 (the U.K., France, Germany) themselves adopted an increasingly hawkish line on Iran, accusing it of destabilizing the region and developing ballistic missiles. The latter charge caused particular indignation in Tehran as these same European countries were increasing the supply of sophisticated arms to Iran’s regional rivals. From Tehran’s perspective, its missiles were vital to national defense.

The lesson for Tehran was unmistakable: Europe might disagree with Washington but it was incapable of protecting the nuclear deal. That inability was arguably a major factor in Tehran’s subsequent pivot to Moscow, which led to it supporting Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine, in exchange for military-technical cooperation — and which, in turn, made EU-Iran relations more adversarial.

The consequences of this failure have become stark during the 2025 and 2026 U.S.-Israeli wars against Iran. Rather than acting as an independent diplomatic bridge capable of mediating between Washington and Tehran, Europe has struggled to define a meaningful role.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wholeheartedly supported the Israeli aggression, notoriously hailing it as Israel doing “the dirty work” for Europeans. The only major European leader who unequivocally opposed the aggression was Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who banned the use of Spanish military bases for the war despite Trump’s attempts to bully Madrid into submission.

Where Europe once led diplomacy with Iran, it is now reduced to issuing bland and toothless statements while Pakistan, Turkey and the Persian Gulf states have stepped in as more consequential diplomatic actors.

The contrast with the approach of 2016 is staggering. The question, then, is not merely how Europe traded its leverage over Iran for moral grandstanding and diplomatic irrelevance, but whether it can recover the understanding of statecraft that once made that leverage possible.

item.title: Ukraine's 'shoot the archer' strategy is far from a silver bullet
item.description:
The story of the Ukraine war is one of “wonder weapons” and their failure to deliver.

First it was HIMARS. Then the Abrams tank. Then F-16s. Then ATACMS. Over and over, Kyiv and its backers have issued urgent demands for a new weapon or capability billed as the key to turning the tide of the war in Ukraine’s favor. Each time, after protesting, the U.S. chose to give in. And each time, the promised silver bullet failed to solve Kyiv’s battlefield challenges.

Now, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and his champions in the U.S. Congress are back with their next request: the intelligence, targeting support, and weapons to find and destroy Russian ballistic missile launchers inside of Russia. As in previous instances, the plan is described as foolproof, an “easy” fix for Ukraine’s air defense challenge, and nearly costless for American taxpayers.

But this new proposal is none of these things. Not only will the plan fail to protect Ukraine’s cities, but it will take another step toward a direct U.S.-Russia war while leaving the U.S. homeland exposed in future conflicts. The Trump administration should dismiss the latest Ukrainian appeal as counter to American interests.

The motives behind Kyiv’s “shoot the archer” strategy are easy to understand. Facing the coming winter with few of the Patriot air defense interceptors that it needs to protect against Russian ballistic missile attacks, Ukraine hopes it can use strikes of its own to disable Russia’s launchers pre-emptively.

The approach is not novel. The Trump administration has adopted the same strategy in its recent campaigns in the Middle East, first against the Houthis and then against Iran, seeking to remove the ability of each adversary to fire missiles at U.S. bases, partners, and commercial ships. Similarly, during the first Gulf War, the U.S. military exerted considerable effort searching for scud missile launchers in the desert to prevent Iraqi attacks on U.S. forces and regional neighbors.

In each of these cases, even with far superior conventional military capabilities and advanced intelligence and weapons, U.S. efforts were much less successful than anticipated or advertised. During the 1991 Gulf War, for example, the U.S. operation involved 1,500 sorties but resulted in few — if any — confirmed successful hits on Iraqi scud missile launchers. The Pentagon instead turned to special forces personnel who roamed the desert looking for the launchers. The U.S. failure to suppress Iranian missile fire has been just as stark. Despite over 10,000 American sorties, Iran still retains 50% of its missile launchers according to some reports, many now hidden underground.

Should Ukraine decide to go after ballistic missile launchers inside of Russia, its challenges would be different from those the U.S. faced in the Middle East. To launch Iskander and other ballistic missiles, Russia relies on mobile systems positioned in regions close to Ukraine, concealed in dense forests, tree lines, or even in old industrial buildings and warehouses. In addition to being hidden, the launchers can travel at fast speeds and across off-road terrain, allowing Russian soldiers to use “shoot-and-scoot” tactics and making it harder for Ukraine to identify and target launchers before their location changes — especially at night, when many Ukrainian operations will occur.

Kyiv has requested from the United States several types of support for its campaign against Russian missile launchers. Its top priority is permission to use Starlink over Russian territory. This capability would, in theory, allow Ukraine to more easily destroy the Russian launchers responsible for ballistic missile attacks by providing targeting, command and control, and counter-electronic warfare support to facilitate Ukrainian drone operations inside Russian territory.

U.S. policy experts have also floated an alternative type of assistance that could facilitate Kyiv’s efforts to hunt Russian missile launchers, suggesting Ukraine could use extended-range attack munitions (ERAM) fired from its F-16s. The United States has already approved the sale of these munitions, but currently Ukraine can only use the missile in its older Soviet aircraft. Ukraine’s F-16s also lack the software and hardware integration needed to dynamically update targeting locations for the ERAM, a necessity for hunting mobile launchers. Upgrading this technology would be fairly straightforward, and this would give Ukraine both the targeting support and munitions it needs to go after Russian launchers.

Either type of support would enhance Ukraine’s ability to prevent ballistic missile attacks at their source, but neither offers anything close to a guarantee of success. Indeed, the fundamental challenges associated with any effort to find and destroy mobile missile launchers would remain.

Ukraine would also face obstacles that the United States did not have to grapple with in Iran. Whereas the United States had the ability to operate across Iranian territory without restrictions, U.S. senators have only asked that Ukraine be given permission to use Starlink 300 km into Russia. Russia’s large size would allow it to simply move launchers outside this range and then continue attacks. On top of this, Ukraine’s limited F-16 fleet is already under strain, lacking sufficient spare parts, waiting for repairs, and facing a shortage of pilots. Ukraine might succeed in destroying some number of Russian launchers, but it is unlikely to prevent severe damage to the country’s cities and infrastructure in the coming winter.

Even if Ukraine could reliably strike Russian missile launchers with a high rate of success, however, giving Kyiv this capability would be a mistake for the United States. Whether it provides more advanced munitions, upgrades Ukraine’s F-16s, or provides Ukraine access to Starlink over Russian territory, enabling Ukraine’s hunt for ballistic missile launchers inside Russia would substantially expand the U.S. role in the war and drag it ever closer to a direct conflict with Russia.

After all, if the Trump administration gives into Kyiv’s demands, Ukraine would be using U.S. intelligence, U.S. satellite networks operating over Russian territory, and possibly U.S. aircraft and weapons to shoot targets inside of Russia. Ukrainians would still be pulling the trigger (or firing the missile or launching the drone), but in all other ways, the mission and its execution would be an American one.

Russia would surely see this as a serious provocation and use it as justification for an expansion of its alleged hybrid campaign against NATO members. This, in turn, could worsen the pre-existing risk of a wider war that drags the United States in, caused by miscalculation or an uncontrolled escalation spiral. Russia might also increase support to Iran or other U.S. competitors by providing weapons and intelligence, putting U.S. forces elsewhere in danger.

Finally, there is the precedent that the United States would set by allowing the use of Starlink over Russian territory. For now, it is only Washington with access to the type of global satellite capability that Starlink provides, but soon Russian and China will have their own networks. Once the United States has allowed the use of Starlink over Russian territory by a third party, there is nothing to stop Moscow or Beijing from making the same decision with their own versions of the technology, leaving the U.S. homeland more vulnerable in the future.

When Ukraine asked for Tomahawk missiles in 2025, the Trump administration wisely broke Biden’s cycle by denying the request on the grounds that stockpiles were too scarce and the capability too escalatory. Trump should do the same today. A campaign to hunt Russian missile launchers would only marginally reduce attacks on Ukraine’s cities and would do so at an unacceptably high cost to American interests in the near and long-term.
