item.title: Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy
item.description:
Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy Expert comment jon.wallace 28 October 2026

The KDP and PUK largely agree on Kurdish issues in Turkey, Iran and Syria. But division on how to govern at home could invite outside interference and undermine hard-won self-governance.

Two years after Iraq’s Kurdistan Region went to the polls to elect a new government, the KDP and the PUK – the region’s two largest parties – have still failed to reach an agreement to form the new government. A caretaker government, originally elected in September 2018, remains in charge.

This situation is taking the Kurdistan Region down a path of profound and possibly permanent division. Its longstanding partners in Europe and the US have grown frustrated with its latent dysfunction and are no longer willing to play referee. This leaves it more vulnerable to interference from regional powers who are better placed to adapt and can play a longer game.

The main impediment to moving forward is not petty disagreements between the two parties over ministerial positions, as is sometimes claimed. Instead, the impasse stems from the collapse of the 2006 Strategic Agreement between the KDP and the PUK. The parties no longer share the same basic vision for how the Kurdistan Region should operate. The formal and informal frameworks that bound the two parties together for the last two decades are no longer functioning.

Instead, the Kurdistan Region has effectively divided into two geographic areas that are controlled by one party or the other. The KDP is in charge in Erbil and Duhok governorates. The PUK is dominant in Sulaymaniyah and Halabja.

The two zones are not fully separate, as they were during the era of divided administrations between 1998 and 2005. But it is a cumbersome arrangement. State institutions and the security forces look to unelected party leaders for guidance, not Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) ministries. Reports indicate that rents are extracted from truckers and traders at checkpoints on the border between KDP and PUK areas.

Until now, the parties have maintained that the Kurdistan Region remains a cohesive entity despite the partisan divide. On 6 October, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani called on the parties to reactivate Kurdistan’s Parliament, which has not had a substantive meeting in more than four years saying: ‘I don’t know what they are afraid of’.

Below the surface, however, bigger changes may be afoot.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

Political leaders from the PUK have a more radical proposal: to devolve administrative and fiscal authority to governorates, mayors, and district directors. Some powers would be retained by the KRG and the Kurdistan Parliament. But most important decisions over everyday matters would be shifted to lower levels of governance. Proponents of the plan cite Switzerland’s cantons and the UAE’s emirates as inspiration. Better to get out of each other’s way, the argument goes, and disaggregate executive authority.

Given the outsized power wielded – exclusively and separately – by the two parties at the governorate and local levels, this change would formalize partisan control over governance within the Kurdistan Region’s two zones, representing the biggest constitutional change in a generation. 

And it would repudiate the key peacebuilding assumption following the Kurdish civil war: that strong, unitary, and shared institutions are needed to reinforce Kurdish self-government and autonomy. That it is even being considered reflects the depths to which relations between the KDP and the PUK have deteriorated.

Many parts of the plan are vague. How would it change the relationship between local authorities, the federal government, and the KRG? How will revenues be shared, if at all? How will decisions be made about key sectors like oil, gas, electricity, and trade?

For the moment this remains a PUK proposal, its prospects uncertain. The KDP opposes the plan – part of the reason there has been little progress in negotiations to form a government. Many Kurdish voters will oppose reinforcing the power of the ruling parties without any meaningful checks. And, while they are certainly disillusioned by their present circumstances, they are keenly aware of the risks the PUK plan would pose to the Kurdistan Region’s fragile constitutional position in Iraq.

Over the past five years, Iraq’s federal government has gradually eroded the KRG’s ability to manage its own political and economic affairs, enabled by the KDP and the PUK disunity. 

A bad time for division

The potential for a fracture inside the Kurdistan Region comes at an inopportune time geopolitically. The US–Iran War has created significant instability. Foreign partners are preoccupied with problems at home. And changing regional dynamics are seeing sovereign states reassert influence over non-state actors.

The US presence in the Kurdistan Region is less potent than in years past. It completed a military withdrawal at the end of September after twelve years as part of the international coalition fighting Islamic State. Diplomatic activity in Erbil – where the KRG is based – has been hampered for much of this year due to security concerns stemming from the US–Iran war.

American and European diplomats are discouraged by their inability to bring the KDP and the PUK together, despite restlessly encouraging them to form a government. This inability is a signal of the West’s flagging influence over top Kurdish leaders. That will only worsen if diplomats have to contend with empowered local officials that answer primarily to the KDP and the PUK leadership.

The Kurdistan Region’s immediate neighbours like Turkey and Iran are much better placed to adapt to a Kurdistan Region that is divided and disaggregated. They can play the long game, and act at the local level through economic, social, and religious ties, rather than the top-down military and political approach of the US and Europe. Unity between the KDP and the PUK matters far less in their calculations.

Turkey’s immediate aim in the Kurdistan Region is to ensure that its own Kurdish political process, which is seeing the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) disarm, continues. The KDP and the PUK have strongly supported this process and provided important interventions to facilitate it. They have also supported the integration process of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the new Syrian state. 

In the near-term, the KDP and the PUK are unlikely to diverge much from this path. But the risk is that greater division at home could fragment their positions on issues beyond the Kurdistan Region’s borders. If that happens, Ankara might side with one of the parties, which would result in further instability.

Iran’s first goal is to ensure that Kurdish groups do not enter its war with the US. So far, the KDP and the PUK are in lockstep about the importance of avoiding any impression that they might intervene against Iran. Tehran’s second goal is to curtail the activities of its own Kurdish armed groups, even to the point of demanding they be expelled from Iraq’s Kurdistan Region. Weak and divided state institutions in the KRG make this difficult to achieve. That, in turn, makes it more likely that Iran will take matters into its own hands.

In the absence of a US security presence, interference from regional neighbours could also lead Iraqi leaders in Baghdad to become more hands-on in dealing with matters in the Kurdistan Region. This would be a bad outcome for Kurdish self-governance and would likely inflame political tensions between the KDP and the PUK.

The sour mood that prevailed in the Kurdistan Region during the election two years ago has only deepened. Pushing governance decisions to the local level in an effort to avoid intractable partisan impasse at the top is one proposal. But it could have significant knock-on effects.  

A continued impasse between the KDP and the PUK risks setting off an irreversible decline for the frameworks that have enabled Kurdish self-governance for the past two decades. To get beyond this blockage, leaders from the KDP and the PUK must entertain imaginative solutions, but not ones that further divide, weaken its shared institutions or undermine democratic principles. Otherwise, it risks becoming a place that other actors pick apart at the expense of Kurdish autonomy.

Whatever the eventual outcome of Israel’s election and next week’s US midterm polls, Donald Trump, playing the Lone Ranger, and Benjamin Netanyahu, his badass Tonto, appear hell-bent on resuming the illegal war of choice they began in June last year and expanded in February. Like a Shakespearean tragedy moving inexorably to a bloody denouement, the worst is yet to come. And yet three things seem certain: the US and Israel will again fail to totally destroy Iran’s largely hypothetical nuclear capabilities; its regime will survive; and millions of ordinary people, there and around the world, will pay the price for this unjustified, reckless aggression.

Ducking and weaving, Trump is desperate to dodge the blame for the Republicans’ anticipated midterm meltdown, largely triggered by war-related fuel and consumer price inflation. He claimed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were responsible, but that didn’t wash. He cut a treacherous diesel deal with Vladimir Putin but, as usual, Russia’s smirking mafioso conned him. He urged US allies to tap their strategic reserves but, unsurprisingly, vilified and sidelined European leaders, who view his war as an unmitigated disaster and declined to bail him out. item.title: Despite intense US pressure, UN votes to condemn Cuba blockade
item.description:
Despite an aggressive U.S. pressure campaign, the United Nations General Assembly voted for the 34th time on Wednesday to condemn the U.S. embargo on Cuba, with 130 nations voting in favor of the resolution, 25 abstaining, and 17 countries, including the U.S. and Israel, voting against.

The Trump administration’s diplomatic push against the annual resolution — spearheaded by U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz — has been even more intense than last year’s. It also came on the heels of similarly unsuccessful efforts this summer by Secretary of State Marco Rubio to shut down a July 7 General Assembly debate on the escalating U.S. economic sanctions against Havana and the humanitarian catastrophe it has precipitated.

While the pressure failed to defeat the measure, it created a notable shift in the vote tally. Compared to last year, an additional 10 states voted against the measure, and an additional 13 states abstained, particularly countries in Latin America and the Caribbean.

Last week, in anticipation of the vote, Waltz hosted a small group of U.S.-backed Cuban dissidents and researchers for an invite-only event making the case against the resolution, citing the island’s political prisoners, foreign medical brigades, corruption, inequality and the military-run monopoly, GAESA. The same day, Waltz hosted a press conference with the CEO of Freedom House titled, “Holding the Cuban Regime Accountable for its Human Rights Abuses,” where he urged other countries’ ambassadors to consider these issues before casting their votes.

In a press conference days before the U.S. media blitz, Cuba’s ambassador to the U.N., Ernesto Soberón, called Waltz’s event the result of Rubio’s “unhealthy obsession with Cuba,” and staged a protest against Waltz and the event panelists along with his colleagues from Cuba’s U.N. mission.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parilla went a step further the following day in Havana, alleging that U.S. officials had threatened tariffs, visa denials for foreign officials and their families, and the suspension of U.S. assistance to countries that did not vote with the United States on Wednesday.

Rodríguez presented no concrete evidence for the claims, but in recent weeks, Rubio publicly pressed Salvadoran president Nayib Bukele, whose country did not participate in last year’s vote, to “join the United States and like-minded partners in advancing shared priorities at the United Nations,” stressing that Cuba’s government “will not make the reforms the Cuban people deserve while it believes the international community is on its side.”

Rubio also recently spoke with the presidents of Panama, Argentina and Colombia — all close allies of the Trump administration — about “regional,” “hemispheric” and U.N.-related issues, though it’s not immediately clear whether the Cuba vote was specifically addressed.

Similar to last year’s push, Waltz invoked the presence of Cubans fighting for Russia in Ukraine to lobby European capitals against supporting Cuba’s U.N. resolution.

In a recent statement, the Cuban government again reiterated its “zero-tolerance policy” against mercenarism, saying that “none of the Cuban citizens who have participated or are participating in any of the parties to this conflict have the encouragement, support, or consent of any Cuban state or government institution.” Authorities say investigations into the recruitment of Cuban citizens abroad to fight in Ukraine have resulted in 43 people being brought before Cuban courts in 12 distinct proceedings, with prosecutors seeking sentences ranging from 5 to 16 years.

Boiling tensions between the longtime adversaries spilled out into the open during the first day of debate this week when Rodríguez Parilla interrupted and approached Ambassador Waltz as he showed images of alleged corruption by Cuban leadership, calling for a point of order.

“He’s not going to intimidate me in the United States of America like he tries to intimidate political prisoners,” Waltz shot back at Rodríguez.

“You are a liar,” Rodríguez retorted.

After a Cuban diplomat tried to prevent one of Waltz’s staffers from filming him as he asked U.N. employees to cut Waltz’s microphone, Waltz told Fox News that Rubio had signed off on the Cuban diplomat’s expulsion from the United States.

While this year’s non-binding vote picked up marginally more support for the U.S. position than in past years, it nonetheless reflected the limits of the administration’s diplomatic arm-twisting — and its null impact on remedying the plight of the Cuban people.

But the State Department’s ratcheted up pressure did not fall flat with everybody. In Europe and the Middle East, Lithuania, Slovenia and the United Arab Emirates broke from their historic position by voting against the resolution, while in Latin America and the Caribbean, Costa Rica, Colombia, Trinidad and Tobago, Honduras and Chile — which have traditionally backed Cuba’s efforts — opposed the resolution or abstained.

Nevertheless, other U.S. allies that have criticized Cuba’s political and economic systems maintained their firm position against the decades-long system of unilateral coercive measures, which, they claim, indiscriminately punishes the Cuban people, violates international law, and discourages reforms related to human rights or the economic system on the island.

“Mexico maintains that the use of unilateral measures as a means of exerting external pressure to influence internal decisions within a sovereign state is incompatible with the principles enshrined in the charter of this organization,” Mexico’s U.N. ambassador Hector Vasconcelos said during the debate.

“The restrictions on fuel exports to Cuba have aggravated the country’s ongoing energy crisis. The shortages have disrupted essential services, including healthcare, education, water supplies, food distribution and transportation,” added India’s representative to the U.N. “India hopes that the embargo will be lifted at the earliest, to help create an environment that would enable the people of Cuba…to pursue their legitimate development aspirations.”

Earlier this year, Cuba presented a report, submitted alongside the draft U.N. resolution, on the impacts of U.S. sanctions on the country’s economy, claiming over $8 billion in losses and damages stemming from maximum pressure U.S. sanctions under the Trump administration.

So far this year, the U.S. has threatened imposing 30% tariffs against countries sending fuel to Cuba, created a new secondary sanctions regime targeting foreign firms operating on the island, and issued dozens of new sanctions and visa restrictions against Cuban officials, ministries, joint ventures, state-owned companies and the country’s fledgling private sector.

The unprecedented squeeze comes amid threats of military and covert action on the island to force regime compliance alongside direct talks between senior U.S. defense, intelligence and policy officials and their Cuban counterparts, as well as reports of back-channel deals and posturing to assume control of Cuba’s key economic assets.

Most recently, on Friday, Rubio called on Cuban leaders to enter into a “discrete partnership” with the CIA — a move seen as an effort to frighten Havana with the specter of covert operations — and Trump said on the campaign trail in Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the war in Iran.

“What we're going to do with Cuba is we're going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Trump said, reiterating a pledge he made five months earlier.

Editor's note: This breaking story was last updated at 11:56 a.m. U.S. Eastern time.

item.title: Why is Egypt jumping into Houthi war? First, follow the money.
item.description:
Egypt's parliament has voted, after two postponements, to authorize President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi to take “necessary measures” to help defend Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, the Iran-aligned group that controls much of Yemen and has spent weeks firing missiles and drones at the kingdom’s airports and fossil fuel infrastructure.

It took weeks of debate in the halls of power for the parliament to ultimately give Sisi the greenlight. This is unusual given that the chamber is largely pro-government and normally gives the president what he asks for.

A handful of members abstained over concerns that relevant details — such as the length of the mission, the cost, how many troops would be sent — were never disclosed. Their complaints reflect deep unease in Egypt about being dragged into a foreign war.

To understand why Sisi has pushed to provide military support to Saudi Arabia, despite institutional reluctance, one must follow the money.

Saudi Arabia keeps roughly $10.3 billion parked at Egypt’s central bank. These deposits count toward Egypt’s foreign-currency reserves. Add accounts owned by Kuwait and Qatar and the total is about $18 billion, close to one-third of Egypt’s $57 billion of reserves. Egypt relies heavily on these deposits because it is one of the world’s biggest wheat importers. It also buys an increasing amount of fuel from abroad and owes billions in interest to foreign lenders, all in dollars, which it does not, on its own, earn enough of.

There is no public indication that Riyadh tied those critical deposits to Egypt’s military support. But Cairo does not need to be asked. Its pound just hit a record low of 56 to the dollar. Debt service — interest plus repayments — takes about 64% of this year’s budget, and the interest payments alone cost more than the state spend on education, health, wages and subsidies put together. A government in this position cannot easily say “no” to one of its main financial backers.

Egypt has spent decades avoiding foreign entanglements, especially in Yemen. In 1962 then-President Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops there to back the republicans in a civil war. The republicans ultimately won, but Egypt was bogged down for years and lost thousands of soldiers.

Yet staying out has proved much harder than Egypt hoped. When Iranian missiles hit the United Arab Emirates earlier this year, Abu Dhabi, which rescued Egypt’s economy in 2024 with a blockbuster $35 billion property deal on the Mediterranean coast, complained loudly that its Arab friends were doing nothing. Cairo then quietly sent a detachment of Rafale fighters, which only became public knowledge when Emirati state media showed Sisi inspecting the jets during a visit.

The lesson learned from that episode is that Gulf money comes with an expectation of visible loyalty.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman (MBS) later flew to Cairo in September, reportedly to ask for help responding to escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom. Egypt’s readout of the meeting was emphatic, framing Saudi security as “an integral part of Egypt’s national security.” But it never named the Houthis or pledged concrete military support. It also paired its rhetorical backing for the kingdom’s security with a call for a political settlement in Yemen.

Six weeks later, Egypt’s parliament has handed Sisi the authority to do more, though he emphasizes that the mission is defensive and “does not include an attack on Yemen.” Cairo’s top diplomat, Badr Abdelatty, has also stressed that “all opportunities for reaching political solutions must be explored.” Cairo is thus trying to provide symbolic support to Riyadh without becoming a party to its war.

This keeps a key backer happy but does nothing for Egypt’s other exposed pillar, the Suez canal, which is one of Egypt’s most important earners of foreign currency, and carries about 12% of world trade.

The canal earned $10.2 billion in 2023, but when the Houthis began attacking Red Sea shipping in solidarity with Gaza and forced vessels to sail around Africa instead, that figure fell to about $4 billion in 2024. The canal authority is hoping for $8 billion in fiscal year 2026/27, but that target assumes the Red Sea calms down — an unlikely prospect at the moment.

Since July, the Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping. In September, they seized the Yemeni ports of Mocha and the island of Mayun, giving them a grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow gateway at the southern end of the Red sea through which every Suez-bound ship must pass.

Cairo reportedly set up a crisis unit and opened channels to the Houthis in response. An Egyptian source told The New Arab those channels were used to press the group to avoid escalation and keep the strait open to shipping. Egypt has little leverage to do more since it formally still belongs to the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally-recognized government, which has prevented Cairo from developing diplomatic channels with the rebel faction.

Above all of this sits the wider war between the U.S., Israel and Iran, now in its eight month. This week, envoys from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — the three members of the Mecca Pact, which Egypt says it is “seriously considering” joining — flew to Tehran to discuss de-escalation. No concrete commitments emerged from the talks.

While Egypt may not have a front-row seat in public diplomacy with Tehran, it is quietly working the backchannels. Abdelatty recently told reporters that Egypt is in daily contact with the Iranians, the Americans and regional states to avoid "full-fledged military clashes which would have a very, very negative impact on the people of the region.”

Abdelatty made these comments as President Donald Trump muses openly about resuming strikes on Iran after the November 3rd midterm elections. Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, reportedly pushed for his own attacks against the backdrop of his own country’s elections, in an apparent bid to complicate his opponent’s efforts to form a government.

A second round of fighting would hurt Egypt more than the first round. The country has already been hit directly: on July 29 a drone struck a floating gas terminal at the port of Damietta and set two vessels on fire. Nobody claimed responsibility, and Egyptian officials never publicly shared their own findings, but renewed fighting could mean more drones and missiles landing on Egyptian soil.

That danger is heightened now that Egypt has formally committed to Saudi Arabia's defense. A senior Houthi figure warned that Cairo’s decision amounts to a “declaration of war” on Yemen, placing Egypt firmly in the line of fire.

Egypt imports a growing share of its gas, and another spike in energy prices would add further pressure to a budget that is already stretched. The Suez Canal is also under increased pressure from the Houthis, who are now better placed to squeeze Red Sea shipping.

Finally, there are remittances — money that Egyptians abroad send home, which help keep Egypt’s foreign-currency reserves and economy afloat. At least 1.25 million Egyptians work in Saudi Arabia alone. The Iran war has already put the Saudi and Gulf economies under strain, and one Iranian official has warned that if Iran is attacked again, “there will be no more red lines.”

Iran has also drawn up plans to hit undersea cables, and its top security official has warned that U.S.-linked data centers and oil facilities across the Gulf could be targeted. Damage on that scale could bring layoffs across the Gulf, changing the math for Egypt’s economy, and stability, very quickly.

item.title: Could the path to US-Iran diplomacy run through Moscow?
item.description:
During a meeting last week with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, Russian President Vladimir Putin offered to help broker a deal to end the U.S.-Iran war.

The proposal — the latest in a series of recent Russian offers to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran — has a certain logic to it. While the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran has brought Russia some economic gains through rising energy prices, Moscow fears further escalation and spillover across the Persian Gulf and parts of the former Soviet space. Russia is also one of Iran’s closest partners and one of the world’s leading exporters of enriched uranium, meaning that it could help break the impasse over domestic Iranian nuclear enrichment.

Yet Moscow will struggle to gain Western and Gulf Arab acceptance as a mediator, particularly amid the Ukraine conflict and heightened threat perceptions of Iran in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) while Russia is increasingly aligned with Iran.

Back in 2022, the balance in the Iran-Russia partnership shifted significantly, with Tehran gaining greater value in Moscow’s eyes as a result of Iranian support to Russia in the form of drones and drone trainers amid its war on Ukraine. Yet now the relationship is shifting in Russia’s favor because of Moscow’s role as an influential power helping Iran weather the war.

“Moscow is trying to provide Iran with every possible form of support,” including grain purchases, humanitarian aid, and likely intelligence sharing, Anton Mardasov, a Moscow-based Associate Fellow at the Middle East Institute, told RS. Mardasov added that this support comes on top of consultations about organizing air defense and missile-development assistance, which were taking place before February 28.

Of course, Moscow’s growing ties with Tehran do not guarantee influence over Iran’s decision making. Its ability to mediate depends on offering Iran and other parties something unavailable elsewhere. According to Mardasov, one avenue is Russia’s longstanding interest in facilitating the transfer of enriched uranium from Iran, potentially followed by support for developing its civilian industrial and nuclear sectors.

Such an arrangement could ease Iran-U.S. tensions, open lucrative contracts, and demonstrate Russia’s diplomatic relevance, potentially strengthening its hand in negotiations over Ukraine. However, Iran has so far shown limited interest in the proposal, constraining its immediate prospects.

Beyond Iran’s reluctance to accept such proposals, other obstacles stand in the way too. Mark Katz, a professor emeritus at George Mason University, said the conditions that facilitated the 2015 Iran deal, known formally as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, are no longer in place.

In the lead-up to the agreement, all parties had interests in a negotiated settlement, allowing Moscow to play a constructive diplomatic role. Today, however, such willingness to compromise appears absent. As Katz explained to RS, “Everyone may want a deal, but not on terms that the opposing party, or parties, is willing to accept.”

Further complicating the picture are the White House’s expectations of Russia. President Donald Trump might expect his Russian counterpart to pressure Tehran into making concessions to Washington just as Putin would want the Trump administration to pressure Kyiv to make concessions to Moscow. If Moscow can’t persuade Iran to adjust its positions, the Kremlin’s value to the White House as a potential intermediary will be limited.

Another open question concerns Russia’s willingness to pressure Iran. Moscow values its partnership with Tehran, and excessive pressure could harm bilateral ties. Putin thus faces a dilemma: Russia must demonstrate enough influence over Iran to appear credible without undermining the Kremlin’s broader international objectives.

Russia’s credibility in the Gulf matters too. While seeking to strengthen ties with GCC members and advance its vision for Gulf security, Russia has complicated its ambitions on the Arabian Peninsula by supporting Iran. Moscow’s opportunistic relationship with Yemen’s Houthi rebel movement, whose attacks on Saudi Arabia exacerbate the regional security crisis, further complicates the Kremlin’s efforts to balance its ties across the Gulf.

“While the GCC states all want good relations with Russia, they know full well that Russian support has helped Iran launch attacks against them. They also know that Moscow is unwilling, and perhaps unable, to pressure Iran to stop attacking them. That being the case, I don't believe the GCC states see Russia as a credible mediator,” Katz told RS.

“In discussions I have had with officials and scholars from the GCC states, contempt for Russia is manifest. Yet they still want to maintain good relations with Moscow for fear that Russia would help Iran even more otherwise,” he added.

These dynamics limit Moscow’s ability to translate its proposed framework for collective security into a reality. When looking at the current state of Russia’s relations with the Gulf Arab monarchies, Mardasov said “Moscow is primarily trying to promote its proposed concept of collective security, which in reality has no real potential and is more of an anti-American project aimed at minimizing the U.S. presence in the region.”

Moscow’s role in the U.S.-Iran conflict is shaped by a gap between Russia’s ambitions and its means to deliver diplomatic results. Although the war has benefited Russia’s economy to some extent and created unique opportunities for Moscow to elevate its partnership with Tehran while reminding the U.S. and other powers of the need to engage Russia, it would be misguided to conclude that any of these dynamics position the Kremlin to resolve this conflict.

Indeed, even if Russia facilitates communication between Tehran and Washington, it is not clear how Moscow could do anything that other bridging states, such as Pakistan, Oman, Qatar, or Turkey, couldn’t if Iran and the U.S. are unwilling to compromise on their core demands.

“Russia can certainly act as an intermediary, relaying messages between Tehran and Washington. But there is no shortage of such intermediaries. Iran and the United States already had fairly reliable channels of communication. In that sense, Russia is unlikely to offer anything fundamentally different from other countries,” Nikita Smagin, a non-resident expert at the state-funded Russian International Affairs Council, told RS.

“The main problem between the United States and Iran is not a lack of mediators, but their inability to find a basis for compromise,” Smagin said. “I doubt Russia can do much to bridge that gap.”

Given Moscow’s support for Iran and its limited leverage over Tehran, it is unclear whether the Kremlin can secure the concessions Washington seeks. Russia may facilitate arrangements, but only if both parties become more willing to compromise. Therefore, for the time being, Moscow will likely be better positioned to leverage this conflict to advance its own geopolitical and economic interests rather than help resolve it.

item.title: Under Trump, the US and Jordan are the best of frenemies
item.description:
Jordan’s relationship with the United States is a tale of two cities.

On the one hand, security cooperation between the two countries is excellent. Thousands of U.S. troops are deployed in the Hashemite Kingdom, with King Abdullah II rebuffing Iranian demands to expel U.S. military installations from the country. Shortly before the Iran war began last February 28 and during its first weeks, the United States transferred many of its soldiers from Arab Gulf countries to perceived safer areas in Jordan.

In September, as Jordanian soldiers conducted a large training exercise with U.S. forces, CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper touted U.S.-Jordan military ties as being “stronger than ever.” Later that month, after the Trump administration withdrew its forces from Iraq, Washington transferred the headquarters of the anti-ISIS military coalition to neighboring Jordan.

Even as President Donald Trump cut foreign aid packages worldwide as part of his “America First” agenda, Washington has increased its assistance to Jordan, a small country with a population of roughly 11.5 million. Congress allocated over $2 billion to the Hashemite Kingdom this year, the third-highest amount across the globe. Since 1951, the United States has provided Jordan approximately $35.5 billion in aid critical to Amman, given its spiraling debt and struggling economy.

The billions in U.S. aid, however, have not translated into a close relationship between Trump and Abdullah. During the Hashemite ruler’s nearly five-week visit to the United States this summer, Abdullah did not get a meeting with the president. Three U.S. soldiers were killed during a July Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, but Trump failed to call the king. Instead, he appeared to criticize Jordan’s military for not intercepting the Iranian missiles. “They did slip something through in Jordan, and if we had other operators, you know, [it] would have not happened,” Trump complained.

The relationship between Trump and Abdullah lacks “chemistry,” Daoud Kuttab, founder of the Amman-based Balad Radio told RS. Trump respects the Qatari and Turkish leaders because of their countries’ wealth and powerful regional roles, Kuttab said. But Abdullah, as the ruler of a poor country, lacks the resources to impress Trump with, for example, a $400 million gifted plane or a massive oil deal.

Dr. Anis Khasawneh, a former vice president at Yarmouk University, told RS that Abdullah fared far better with former President Joe Biden. In contrast to Trump, Biden imposed some sanctions on Israeli settlers in the West Bank, whose fate is of keen interest to Abdullah, according to Khasawneh, a key Jordanian concern given its borders with the West Bank and desire for stability there. Palestinians, including some two million refugees, make up roughly half of Jordan’s population. (Trump immediately lifted all of Biden’s settler sanctions on his return to office last year.)

During Trump’s first term, the president ignored Abdullah’s appeals not to move the U.S. embassy in Israel to Jerusalem; their last bilateral meeting in the first term took place in July 2018, and no meeting was held until after Trump initially left office in 2021. And in his second term, Trump has pressed Abdullah on particularly sensitive issues, urging the king to absorb displaced Gazans.

While the United States planned with Israel extensively for its attack against Iran, there is no media reporting that Trump alerted Abdullah beforehand even though the war sparked barrages of Iranian missiles targeting Jordan. “There is a growing feeling in Jordan that Washington, particularly under President Trump, is underestimating Jordan’s regional role and no longer attaches the same political importance to the country, as it did in previous decades,” former Jordanian minister Mohammad Abu-Rumman told RS.

Jennifer Sutton, a spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Amman, declined an interview request with Amb. James Holtsnider.

In addition to the mistrust between the two leaders, Jordanian public opinion is increasingly critical of U.S. policies in the region. According to an Arab Barometer poll, only 12% of Jordanians view Trump’s foreign policy favorably.

Saad Hattar, an Amman-based political analyst, contended that Jordanians believe “the United States has always been the cause of misery and hardship for the people in the region, especially the Palestinians.” Given that about half of Jordan’s population is of Palestinian origin, the Trump administration’s support for Israeli actions in the West Bank and Gaza angered Jordanians, added Hattar.

Trump’s war against Iran only heightened Jordanians’ alienation. Led by former minister Amjad al-Majali, hundreds of Jordanians signed a July letter calling for the expulsion of U.S. troops from the Hashemite Kingdom. “We maintain that their presence exposes Jordan to security, political, and economic risks that serve no interest and increase the likelihood of our country being dragged into a regional conflict to which it is not a party,” the letter stated.

Before this year, the U.S. military presence in Jordan posed virtually no risks to the country. But this quickly changed after Trump ordered the assault against Tehran, and the Islamic Republic responded by launching missiles and drones at U.S. forces in Jordan.

Since Jordanian public opinion remains hostile to Washington and Trump’s relationship with Abdullah lacks warmth, to say the least, why does the United States continue to provide billions in aid to Amman?

The king has prioritized outreach to Capitol Hill — both Democrats and Republicans — since ascending to the throne in 1999. Such congressional coordination, along with deep ties with the U.S. military and CIA, has ensured that key voices in the U.S. government continue to advocate for Jordan, even with reduced White House support. In addition, the Iran war has further highlighted Jordan’s strategic value to the U.S. security establishment as the Hashemite kingdom continues to host additional U.S. troops despite the risks of further attacks by Tehran and militias allied with it in Iraq. (No polls have been released on U.S. public attitudes regarding aid to Amman.)

“The paradox is that King Abdullah remains one of Washington’s most reliable regional allies,” Abu-Rumman explained. “Yet he may feel more politically distant from the current American president than from many of his predecessors.”

item.title: Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose
item.description:
Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose  Expert comment jon.wallace 29 October 2026

Either way, the UK will be forced to pay a price.

The EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) is pushing the UK toward an economic confrontation with China it would rather avoid. The IAA plans to introduce new ‘Made in Europe’ obligations, conditioning access to certain public subsidy and procurement schemes on the use of sufficient local, European, content. This is intended, in part, to protect European industry from cheap, high-quality, Chinese goods such as hybrid and electric vehicles (EVs). 

The UK government, seeking closer economic integration with the EU, wants ‘Made in Europe’ provisions extended to include its firms. But key EU member states are conditioning any extension on the UK aligning with EU economic security measures. 

A 15 October Franco-German paper said that ‘Made in Europe’ treatment for the automotive sector should only be extended to the UK and a small group of other partners on the condition of both reciprocity and ‘dynamic alignment with EU conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defense measures’. 

In practical terms, France and Germany want the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese EVs to prevent the further erosion of their manufacturers’ UK market share. They also want the UK to impose stricter conditions on foreign direct investment into key manufacturing sectors to prevent Chinese firms from qualifying for future EU subsidies or procurement schemes via their UK-located operations. 

With the next EU–UK summit scheduled for 20 November, this creates a problem for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new government. Much of the media reporting has focused on the question of whether the UK will agree to impose tariffs on Chinese vehicles. But the focus on investment is arguably more consequential, given the UK’s desire to attract Chinese automotive manufacturing facilities to Britain. 

The UK’s China problem

Until now, the UK’s preferred approach to China has been one of cautious pragmatism. It has demonstrated a willingness to intervene with tariffs or other restrictions in the event of acute economic or national security concerns. See, for example, the decision to impose permanently high tariffs on certain steel products or the blocking of a proposed £1.5 billion investment in offshore wind by the Chinese firm Ming Yang. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

However, the UK has continued to court Chinese investment in the automotive sector and deepen trade ties in what it considers non-sensitive areas. And, though it has made a commitment to the US to strengthen supply chain security in respect of steel and pharmaceuticals as part of the 2025 Economic Prosperity Deal, there has so far been limited evidence of substantive implementation. 

The UK’s reluctance to fully align with either the EU or US approach to China is understandable, given its relative size and economic weight. It wants increased trade and investment and relies on Chinese renewables for its decarbonization objectives. 

But the UK can certainly not afford to be shut out of EU procurement and public subsidy schemes. The EU’s proposed safeguard on hybrid vehicle imports – which would restrict imports above specified quota levels – will also create its own pressures, as Chinese vehicles risk being diverted onto the UK market. 

It is therefore less of a question of whether the UK will align itself with EU economic security measures than how.

The price to pay

One route would be for the UK to replicate EU measures wholesale. This would see the UK replicate EU tariffs on EVs and the new hybrid safeguard. And it could potentially include future interventions targeting chemicals, plastics, batteries and wind turbines. 

The UK would also need to consider equivalent restrictions on foreign investment, reflecting proposed IAA conditions relating to ownership limits, joint ventures, workforce localization and local content in key manufacturing sectors. 

Yet this approach is not straightforward. The UK does not necessarily have the legal tools available to replicate EU measures and has historically been cautious about breaching its international obligations. 

China would also be incentivized to retaliate. That could mean anything from initiating its own tariff measures against UK exports to imposing restrictions on rare earths or battery inputs.

The UK is not the only country in the region facing pressure from the EU to impose more stringent controls on Chinese trade and investment as a condition for access to the EU market. Turkey, Morocco and Switzerland are in a similar position. China will be wary of a negative precedent being established and keen to demonstrate that aligning with EU restrictions comes at a price. Indeed, Beijing may have a greater incentive to make an example of the UK than escalate its confrontation with the EU.

An alternative would be for the UK to pursue similar outcomes more slowly, using traditional trade defence tools. An anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese electric vehicles, for example, would take around a year to conclude but could provide the government with some breathing space. A safeguard investigation, potentially justified by rising Chinese imports and the risk of trade diversion from the EU, could offer a quicker route. 

Neither would guarantee the outcome the EU wants. And both would need to satisfy the relevant legal requirements. But they would at least allow the UK to argue that it was responding to evidence of harm to its own industry, rather than simply implementing EU demands. 

A safeguard also has the benefit, or not, of generally applying to imports regardless of origin, allowing the UK to argue it is not singling out China. It also remains possible that Brussels will attach more importance to the political signal of alignment than to the precise form of the measures adopted.

Yet this still leaves open the question of Chinese investment into UK manufacturing. This is of particular importance in the automotive sector. And it will prove more difficult to address without compromising the government’s wider economic objectives.

The government could also seek to demonstrate progress by announcing new economic security tools, such as a proposed anti-coercion instrument. It could also introduce specific restrictions on foreign investment, or repackage existing initiatives, such as new cybersecurity-related restrictions. Such announcements might demonstrate goodwill towards Brussels but they would not automatically satisfy EU demands for alignment on specific measures. 

The most likely outcome is that the UK seeks to navigate a course through these competing demands, giving the EU just enough of what it wants, while delaying implementation, hoping to avoid the worst response from Beijing. Delay may buy time with Brussels. But Beijing will likely view any such commitment as setting a precedent and retaliate against the UK accordingly. 

There will be a price for the UK to pay either way. The only question is how successfully the government can minimize it.

Trump wants Myanmar's rare earths. He's talking to the wrong people.
item.description:
The Trump administration is carrying out a major shift in U.S. policy toward Myanmar.

After the 2021 coup, the administration of former President Joe Biden demanded a return to democracy and sanctioned the military junta. Now, however, Washington is reportedly holding direct talks with the very people it accused of genocide in 2022.

Trump had already given Gen. Min Aung Hlaing implicit recognition when he sent him a tariff letter in July 2025. Two weeks later, the U.S. Treasury removed several of his cronies from its sanctions list. In June this year, officials from both countries met in Tokyo. But the most significant step came in mid-September, when Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance opened direct talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw, Myanmar’s capital, marking the highest-level U.S. contact since the coup.

The stated goals of U.S. reengagement are narrow: securing the release of U.S. businessman Adam Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, and enlisting the regime’s cooperation in shutting down the online scam centers operating in the country. U.S. officials also had their eyes on Myanmar's rare earth deposits, a market currently controlled by China.

The first goal has been achieved. On the second, the regime is part of the problem, and the third lies in territory it does not control. So is Trump betting on a partner that cannot deliver?

A bogged-down war


The current phase of the war began in mid-2021 when the crackdown on anti-coup protests pushed thousands of activists into the countryside where minority insurgencies had been operating for decades. Alongside the armed resistance, ousted lawmakers from the National League for Democracy, the ruling party prior to the coup, creating the National Unity Government (NUG). While some militant groups joined the NUG, others remained independent. The result is a conflict fragmented both politically and geographically, whose actors pursue different goals, shift alliances and tactics, and are tied to different foreign powers.

Over the following four years, the military lost control of much of the country to the NUG and ethnic armed organizations while keeping its grip on the main levers of the economy, such as ports, factories and offshore gas. But it lost access to most rare earth deposits, which are now held by minority groups like the Wa, Karens and Shan.

The Biden administration responded with targeted sanctions on the junta’s leaders and its business conglomerates, and supported pro-democracy groups through humanitarian and non-lethal aid, much of it channeled across the Thai border. There were never any weapons transfers or formal recognition of the NUG as a legitimate interlocutor.

Aid from the United States and Europe, said Khun Alynn, Deputy Head of Department of Home Affairs, Interim Executive Council of Karenni State (IEC), “came through humanitarian organizations, but also through third countries that I can’t confirm.”

Then, in 2025, the incoming Trump administration dismantled USAID, just as the military launched a counteroffensive and began retaking territory with new tactics and drones supplied by Russia and China.

“The [USAID] cuts had a huge impact. Medical supplies are already running short, and we can’t deal with the malaria and tuberculosis outbreaks in the area. At least two hospitals are going to close by the end of the year,” Paung, a 35-year-old doctor and director of the Luke Foundation, told Responsible Statecraft.

Five years of war have taken a staggering toll: according to the UN, more than 3.7 million people are internally displaced, and violence monitor ACLED has recorded 100,114 conflict-related deaths. In Karenni, Maw Re Ree, deputy head of the IEC's humanitarian department, works in the region's roughly 500 displacement camps. "We systematically receive threats of bombing," she said.

Sovereignty problems


The junta retains formal sovereignty but controls only about 21% of Myanmar’s territory; resistance forces hold some 42%, and the rest is contested. To consolidate his position, in January 2026, Min Aung Hlaing held an election in only those parts of the country that were under his control and was sworn in as president of a nominally civilian government in a ceremony attended by representatives of China, India and Thailand, along with 20 other countries, last April. Western governments dismissed the vote as a sham, while Washington stayed silent.

That silence has left the opposition uneasy, especially in light of the administration’s recent moves. “The military regime may also seek to use engagement with the United States to overcome its crisis of political legitimacy,” Zin Mar Aung, the NUG’s foreign minister, told Responsible Statecraft.

Washington’s priority appears to be curbing the financial losses and the harm to Americans caused by online scams and drug trafficking. The scam compounds, located near the Thai border, are run by criminal syndicates and protected by junta-allied militias, such as the Border Guard Forces, which receive financial kickbacks from the scammers. Given this relationship and the power of the criminal syndicates, the regime “cannot fully guarantee” an end to these practices, Zin Mar Aung noted.

Rare earths, meanwhile, are “entirely off-limits to Naypyidaw,” said David Gum Awng, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister, referring to Myanmar’s capital.

Indeed, in late 2024, the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) seized the heart of one of the world's most valuable concentrations of heavy rare earths, and it taxes the trade with China to fund its fight. Further east, in territory controlled by the United Wa State Army (UWSA), which has remained neutral in the ongoing civil war, Chinese companies are mining rare earths, also without Naypyidaw's approval.

The options floated in Washington have ranged from dealing with the military authorities to brokering talks between them and the KIA, to engaging the KIA directly and possibly partnering with India to process the minerals. Each of those paths runs through Naypyidaw or bypasses the opposition coalition, which narrows the resistance’s room for maneuver without forcing an open break.

“So we're taking it very cautiously, but we also understand the very pragmatic nature of the world order that we live in,”said David Gum Awng, who noted that the NUG still maintains some contact with Washington.

The cost of the bet


For Napas Thein, a research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Myanmar Policy and Community Knowledge Hub, engaging the junta would cost Washington “credibility regarding democracy and human rights” and draw it into a highly unstable landscape. It would also strain U.S. ties with the resistance groups that control much of the country, and bring it closer to a regime aligned with Iran and North Korea.

What can the United States gain from a government that is partly financed by a criminal economy and does not control rare earths mines, Washington’s chief interest? The answer remains unclear.

Meanwhile, the war continues to drag on, and civilians continue to suffer. Just recently, a regime airstrike killed 50 people, including women and children, in a town in rebel-held Rakhine state.

item.title: Qatari mediators return to Tehran to push for US-Iran deal, official says
item.description:
Oct 30 (Reuters) - Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of efforts to reach a deal between the US and Iran, an official briefed on the talks told Reuters.

The mediation talks have been coordinated with the US, the official said.

Qatar presented a draft peace plan to Iran on Sunday, according to an official briefed on negotiations. But a senior Iranian official dismissed the proposals as unacceptable and said Tehran would maintain its nuclear position.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis deny launching drone after coalition reports interception in Mecca region
item.description:
Oct 30 (Reuters) - Yemen's Houthis denied launching any attack towards Saudi Arabia on Friday, after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by the group over the Mecca region.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree dismissed the coalition's account as false in a post on X, saying the group had not carried out any operation towards Saudi territory. He said its operations target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
